name: domain-service
intent: Model a significant domain operation - transfer, allocation, conversion - that is not a natural part of any single Entity or Value Object as a standalone, stateless service: declare its interface in the language of the model, make the operation name part of the ubiquitous language, and use it judiciously so services never strip entities and value objects of their behaviour.
problem: Some operations of the ubiquitous language - transferring funds, allocating cargo, pricing a basket, converting money - span several model elements and fit none of them: attaching the operation to an arbitrary entity turns that object into a script for someone else's job, and scattering it across callers leaves the rule unnamed and unowned. The recurring decision is whether to force the operation onto an object that does not really own it, or to model it explicitly as a service.
context: Model-driven design (Domain Model, Aggregate, Entity and Value Object) where behaviour is expected to live with the data it works on: the operation is a verb of the ubiquitous language, combines several entities or value objects (or a policy none of them owns), has no per-client state, and is invoked from a use case or from another model element. Typical in the domain layer of a layered or hexagonal architecture, with its collaborators declared as domain-owned abstractions.
benefits: Gives operations that span several model elements a named home in the model, instead of a 'phony object' or a method on an arbitrary entity that does not really own the rule.
Keeps entities and value objects focused on their own invariants; the dense network of associations that grows when one object has to serve many beneficiaries disappears.
The operation's name and interface come from the ubiquitous language, so the concept stays visible to domain experts and to the code's readers.
Statelessness makes the service shareable - one instance serves every client, with no per-client history to synchronise - and trivially testable with substituted collaborators.
Cross-aggregate policies (allocation, pricing, conversion, identity generation) get a single owner, which removes duplication between callers and keeps the rule consistent.
The interface is declared in model terms and the implementation behind it is replaceable, so algorithms and policies can vary without changing callers.
tradeoffs: Overuse erodes the model: services absorb behaviour that belonged on entities and value objects, producing an anemic domain model plus service bloat.
Deciding that an operation belongs to no object is a judgement call; a wrong call hides behaviour away from the data it works on and is harder to follow than a well-placed entity method.

Statelessness is a convention, not a language guarantee - caches, lazily-initialised collaborators or request-scoped fields creep in and quietly break shareability (Evans himself later relaxed the rule).

The boundary against the Application Service and the infrastructure service is easy to miss: services that own transactions, map DTOs or reach into frameworks are application services in disguise, and the domain layer slowly depends on the outside world.
Fine-grained services multiply indirection: understanding one rule means following calls out of the entity into a service and back, and debugging spans more objects.
The name is overloaded - Service collides with Service Layer, Service-Oriented Architecture and 'service' as an infrastructure concept - so teams frequently place the operation in the wrong layer.

participants.responsibility: Declares the standalone domain operation as an interface expressed in terms of the model - parameters and results are domain objects - and carries its name into the ubiquitous language.
Any model element or application service that needs the operation; it depends on the service's interface, never on a concrete implementation or the service's internals.

The abstractions the operation needs to do its work - a repository of an aggregate, a policy, a rate source, a clock - declared and owned by the domain layer so no infrastructure type leaks into the interface.
The operands and results: the service reads and produces them, must not retain them as state, and must not be their owner.

use_cases: Funds transfer between two accounts, including the interbank and clearing steps that are no single Account's responsibility (Evans' canonical example).
Cargo allocation: assigning shipments to voyages with a routing and capacity algorithm that walks the whole cargo/voyage graph.
Currency conversion or fee and interest calculation driven by rates and policies shared across many accounts and products (Vernon's calculation-process service).
Generating a unique, human-meaningful identifier - invoice number, order number, policy number - whose format spans several aggregates.
Evaluating a basket-level discount or eligibility rule that combines products, customer history and promotions before any aggregate is mutated.
Answering a domain question that needs several aggregates in one consistent decision, such as whether a customer may reserve this cargo.
Inventory reservation: checking availability across multiple warehouse locations and reserving stock before order confirmation — spans Product, Warehouse, and Reservation aggregates.
Credit limit evaluation: determining whether a customer can place an order based on their outstanding balance, credit terms, and current order value — crosses Customer, Order, and Pricing aggregates.
Route optimisation: calculating the best delivery route given constraints on vehicle capacity, time windows, and driver availability (Microsoft Azure drone-delivery Scheduler example).

Tax calculation for cross-border transactions: computing applicable taxes given the seller's jurisdiction, buyer's jurisdiction, product category, and current treaty rates — involves multiple fiscal policy value objects.
Fraud scoring: evaluating a transaction against patterns stored across Account, Session, and History aggregates to assign a risk score before authorisation.
Merging duplicate customer records: identifying and consolidating two Customer aggregates into one, transferring all associated Order and Contact references atomically.
Commission calculation for a multi-tier sales representative hierarchy: traversing the rep tree, applying different rates at each level, and producing a Commission value object.

Assigning an issue to a user with a per-assignee open-limit check that needs a repository count and mutates the Issue aggregate - ABP Framework's canonical IssueManager domain service, registered stateless with a transient DI lifetime.

Annotating service-layer classes with Spring Framework's @Service stereotype, whose Javadoc defines the role verbatim in Evans' terms - 'an operation offered as an interface that stands alone in the model, with no encapsulated state'.

Funds transfer as a banking domain service that interacts with Account and Ledger objects, making debits and credits and confirming whether the transfer was allowed (Evans' worked example in Chapter 5)
avoid_when: The operation naturally fits an existing entity or value object: put the method there; a service is the exception, not the default.
Only orchestration is needed (load, invoke, persist, publish, commit): that is an Application Service or a Service Layer, and it carries use-case flow rather than business rules.
The work is technical - persistence, messaging, email, caching: model it as an infrastructure gateway or adapter, not as a domain service.
A single trivial operation with one collaborator and no domain vocabulary to express is all that is at stake: a plain method or function on the model element is simpler.
The application really is procedural CRUD with little behaviour: a Transaction Script is more honest than a thin model decorated with services.
anti_patterns: Service per entity: <Entity>Service classes that only forward CRUD and validation, leaving the entities anemic.
Stateful service: caches, session data or lazily-initialised objects stored as fields, so behaviour depends on call history and the instance can no longer be shared.
A 'domain' service that owns the transaction, DTO mapping, authorization and logging - an Application Service wearing a domain name.
Interface defined in infrastructure terms (ORM entity, SQL session, HTTP client), which drags the domain layer into depending on the outside world.
God service: one class accumulating every operation that touches a subsystem, with no cohesion and an ever-growing dependency list.
Void/boolean service: the operation mutates whatever it was handed and returns nothing, hiding the outcome instead of returning a domain result.
Service becoming a garbage bin: all cross-aggregate logic dumped into one service until it has dozens of unrelated methods and dependencies.
Query混入command: adding read methods (findBy, getAll) to a domain service that should only perform state-changing operations.
Transaction ownership: the service opens or commits its own database transaction instead of participating in one opened by the caller.
Adaptor direct dependency: calling an infrastructure adaptor (HTTP client, ORM session) from the domain layer instead of through a domain-owned port.
design_principles: Single responsibility and high cohesion: one domain activity per service, named after the verb of the ubiquitous language.
Separation of concerns: domain rules in the domain layer, use-case orchestration and transactions in the application layer.
Dependency inversion: collaborators are abstractions owned by the domain and injected from outside.
Information hiding: parameters and results are domain objects; the algorithm is private to the service.
Statelessness as a design invariant: the service is a pure fabrication that holds behaviour with no home in the model, so it can be shared freely.
Low coupling: a service dissolves the association web that would otherwise grow between entities and the many objects they serve.
best_practices: Push the operation onto an entity or value object first and introduce a service only when it genuinely spans model elements (Vernon: 'Make Sure You Need a Service').
Name the service and its operations from the ubiquitous language (a verb phrase such as FundsTransfer#transfer) and define the interface in terms of domain objects.
Keep it stateless: no mutable fields, collaborators injected read-only, results returned rather than retained.
Declare the interface in the domain layer and keep infrastructure types out of its signature; add the separated interface only when substitution is genuinely expected.
Return domain results or fail with domain-specific errors instead of void or bare booleans, so callers see the outcome.
Let the application service own the unit of work, the transaction boundary and the DTO mapping.
Test with in-memory fakes of the collaborators: a domain service must be testable without a container, a database or a network.
Return domain results or domain-specific errors rather than void or bare booleans so callers can see the outcome without exceptions for expected cases.

Declare collaborators as domain-owned abstractions (repository interfaces, policy ports, rate sources, clocks) injected at the composition root — never let infrastructure types leak into the service signature.

Prefer a concrete stateless class over a separated interface unless you genuinely need multiple implementations or infrastructure-based substitution (separated interface is a choice, not a necessity per Vernon).
Never let the service open or commit transactions — that is the Application Service's job; the domain service participates in the unit of work already opened by its caller.
Domain services that span multiple aggregates should be wrapped by an Application Service that manages the unit of work so all changes commit atomically.

Use domain abstractions (interfaces) for external integrations (e.g. IInventoryChecker, IExchangeRateProvider) defined in the domain layer, with implementations in infrastructure — this keeps the domain independent of technical details.
If a service method must handle exceptions from collaborators, catch and re-throw as domain-specific errors rather than letting raw infrastructure exceptions escape.

Name service methods with business verbs that match the ubiquitous language (e.g. AssignToAsync, ChangePriceAsync, Transfer) — avoid generic names like UpdateAsync or ProcessAsync that carry no domain meaning.
Keep domain services focused on one business concept — if the service name must include 'And' or 'With', it is probably two services.
Avoid stateful collaborators (e.g. a cached rate provider holding live data as a field) — inject a stateless provider that reads on-demand, or pass the data as a method argument.

For related-pattern context: Application Services orchestrate use cases and own the transaction boundary; they call Domain Services when a cross-aggregate operation is needed. The most common mistake is swapping the two — Application Services grow fat with domain logic (producing an anemic domain model) while Domain Services stay thin.

For related-pattern context: Service Layer (Fowler, PoEAA) is the umbrella pattern encompassing both Application Services and Domain Services. Fowler's 'domain facade' approach keeps the Service Layer thin over a rich Domain Model; Evans' Domain Service is one specific kind of service within this layer.

For related-pattern context: Domain Services should be the exception — most behaviour belongs on entities and value objects. When all behaviour migrates into services leaving entities as data bags, the model has become anemic (Fowler's Anemic Domain Model anti-pattern), incurring all the costs of a Domain Model without any of the benefits.

For related-pattern context: Entities own behaviour that relates to their own lifecycle and invariant. A Domain Service takes behaviour that spans multiple entities. Heuristic: if the verb applies to a single noun, make it an entity method; if it applies to several nouns, it is a Domain Service.

For related-pattern context: Aggregates define transactional consistency boundaries; a Domain Service operates across those boundaries. The Application Service wraps Domain Service calls in a unit of work to keep cross-aggregate changes consistent.

For related-pattern context: A Specification encapsulates complex validation or selection criteria. Domain Services commonly receive Specification objects as collaborators and apply them across collections of entities.

For related-pattern context: Domain Services use Strategy to delegate variant behaviour (e.g. different pricing algorithms per customer tier). Strategy implementations must live in the domain layer; only the selection and delegation logic lives in the service.

For related-pattern context: Transaction Script is a simpler procedural pattern for low-complexity logic. When Domain Services absorb too much logic that could live on entities, the model tips toward Transaction Script with objects on top.
sources: Evans, Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software (2003) - Services, in Chapter 5, A Model Expressed in Software: an operation offered as an interface that stands alone in the model, with no encapsulated state; the three characteristics of a good service ('the operation relates to a domain concept that is not a natural part of an Entity or Value Object', the interface is defined in terms of other model elements, the operation is stateless); the funds-transfer example.

In the shipping bounded context, the Scheduler functions as a domain service because the scheduling logic involves business rules about drone availability, delivery windows, and route optimization that don't belong to any single entity.'

Martin Fowler, Evans Classification (2005): https://martinfowler.com/bliki/EvansClassification.html — 'A standalone operation within the context of your domain. A Service Object collects one or more services into an object. Typically you will have only one instance of each service object type within your execution context.' Fowler also notes Evans later relaxed the statelessness requirement.

ABP Framework, What is That Domain Service in DDD (2024): https://abp.io/community/articles/what-is-that-domain-service-in-ddd-for-.net-developers-uqnpwjja — 'A Domain Service represents a domain concept that doesn't naturally belong to a single Entity or Value Object, but still belongs to the domain layer - not to the application or infrastructure.'

ABP Framework, Application Services vs Domain Services: https://abp.io/community/articles/app-services-vs-domain-services-4dvau41u — 'Domain Services implement core business logic and are particularly needed when: logic spans multiple aggregates, or the business logic is related to more than one aggregate/entity and doesn't properly fit in any single aggregate.'

Xebia, Domain-Driven Design Part 2 — Application Services and Domain Services (2016): https://xebia.com/blog/domain-driven-design-part-2-application-services-and-domain-services/ — 'Domain Services must follow the Ubiquitous Language and are part of the Domain layer. A Domain Service is often used whenever a given operation must access more than one Aggregate Root.'

Marko Milojevic, Practical DDD in TypeScript: Domain Service (Plain English, 2023): https://javascript.plainenglish.io/practical-ddd-in-typescript-domain-service-8c32afefb102 — 'Domain Service IS NOT ALLOWED to hold a state. This is probably the most important rule in all Tactical DDD patterns. Domain Service represents behaviors from Problem Domain. It provides solutions for business invariants that are too complex to be stored inside a single Entity or Value Object.'

Stack Overflow, Right and Wrong About Services in DDD (2019): https://stackoverflow.com/questions/56968565/right-and-wrong-about-services-in-ddd — 'Domain services are the true API of the domain. They contain domain logic, work only with domain objects, usually contain code that orchestrates different aggregates, and are part of a domain's ubiquitous language.'

BestHub, 10 Common DDD Mistakes and How to Avoid Them (2026): https://www.besthub.dev/articles/10-common-ddd-mistakes-and-how-to-avoid-them-010696673239 — Anti-Pattern 5: 'Domain Service Becomes a Garbage Bin, Dumping All Logic Inside. Correct approach: place business methods on the aggregate root whenever they affect only that aggregate; reserve Domain Services for truly cross-aggregate coordination or stateless algorithms.'

Spring Framework, @Service annotation Javadoc: https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/docs/current/javadoc-api/org/springframework/stereotype/Service.html — 'Indicates that an annotated class is a "Service", originally defined by Domain-Driven Design (Evans, 2003) as "an operation offered as an interface that stands alone in the model, with no encapsulated state."'

ABP Framework, Domain Services (official docs): https://abp.io/docs/latest/framework/architecture/domain-driven-design/domain-services — 'the core business logic is generally implemented in aggregates (entities) and the Domain Services. Creating a Domain Service is especially needed when... the logic you need to implement is related to more than one aggregate/entity, so it doesn't properly fit in any of the aggregates'; DomainService/IDomainService base classes, transient DI registration, Manager naming convention, IssueManager example.

ABP Framework, Domain Services Best Practices & Conventions: https://abp.io/docs/latest/framework/architecture/best-practices/domain-services — define domain services in the domain layer, no interface without good reason, Manager suffix, no GET methods (use the repository from the Application Service instead), no DTO returns, no authenticated-user logic inside the service.

FedWiki, Services (free DDD pattern wiki): http://ddd.fed.wiki.org/services.html — 'When a significant process or transformation in the domain is not a natural responsibility of an Entity or Value Object, add an operation to the model as a standalone interface declared as a Service... Make the Service stateless.'

Vladimir Khorikov (@emacsway), Design of Service Layer and Application Logic: https://emacsway.github.io/en/service-layer/ — extended Evans quotation with the three characteristics of a good service, the domain/application/infrastructure service boundary (funds transfer vs. spreadsheet export vs. e-mail notification), and the warning that 'SERVICES should be used judiciously and not allowed to strip the ENTITIES and VALUE OBJECTS of all their behavior'.

Martin Fowler, Anemic Domain Model (2003): https://martinfowler.com/bliki/AnemicDomainModel.html — the misuse critique: domain objects reduced to 'bags of getters and setters' with 'a set of service objects which capture all the domain logic', designs that 'incur all of the costs of a domain model, without yielding any of the benefits'.

Vernon, Implementing Domain-Driven Design - official Pearson sample pages: https://ptgmedia.pearsoncmg.com/images/9780321834577/samplepages/0321834577.pdf — contents confirming Chapter 7 'Services' with 'Transformation Services' and 'Using a Mini-Layer of Domain Services'.
